intro: Use standard library functions with their headers, valid domains, and argument contracts. Mathematical results and character classification both require more care than matching a function name.
outcomes: Use common math and character functions.
Handle EOF and signed characters correctly.
prerequisites: A function call passes arguments and obtains a return value. A header declares the interface. Floating-point arithmetic represents many values approximately; a character code is a numeric representation of a character.

sections.title: 1. Mathematical library
paragraphs: <math.h> declares sqrt, pow, fabs, floor, ceil, round, sin, cos, log, and other functions. sqrt(x) computes a square root for a nonnegative real input. log(x) is the natural logarithm and needs positive real input. Trigonometric functions take radians, not degrees.

floor rounds toward negative infinity; ceil toward positive infinity; round rounds to the nearest integer value with halfway cases away from zero. These functions return floating values. For -2.7, floor gives -3.0 and ceil gives -2.0. A cast to int truncates toward zero when the truncated value is representable.

pow is a floating-point power function; ^ is bitwise XOR, not exponentiation. abs in <stdlib.h> is for int, while fabs is for double. abs(INT_MIN) cannot be represented when the negative range has one extra magnitude. Check input ranges even for familiar library functions.
example: Expected lines are root=9.0 power=8.0; floor=-3.0 ceil=-2.0 round=-3.0; alpha=1 upper=A in the default C locale. Some GCC systems need -lm when linking this example; place it after the source/object arguments.

sections.title: 2. Character classification and conversion
paragraphs: <ctype.h> provides isalpha, isdigit, isspace, isalnum, isupper, islower, toupper, and tolower. Classification returns zero for false and a nonzero value for true; do not assume the true result is exactly 1. Locale can affect classifications and case mappings.

Each ctype argument must be EOF or a value representable as unsigned char. A plain char can be negative. For a character stored in char c, use isalpha((unsigned char)c). This cast prevents negative byte values from violating the function contract.

getchar returns int so it can represent both byte values and EOF. Keep that result in int, test EOF before converting to a byte, and then classify it. These functions classify single byte values; they are not a complete Unicode text-processing system.

sections.title: 3. Domains, approximation, and testing
paragraphs: Before calling sqrt for a real calculation, reject negative inputs. Before log, reject zero and negative inputs. Checking the domain keeps error handling part of the algorithm rather than depending on a surprising result. math_errhandling describes library error-reporting support; domain failures can involve errno and/or floating exceptions.

Floating-point equality is suitable when equality of the represented values is actually intended, but approximate numerical algorithms need a tolerance justified by their scale and error model. A fixed magic tolerance is not universally valid.

Test positive, zero, and negative inputs where meaningful. For character functions test a letter, a digit, a space, and EOF. Do not use a negative char experiment as if its invalid library call had a defined answer.

revision: Match functions to headers and argument types.

questions.question: Is 2 ^ 3 equal to eight in C?
answer: No. ^ performs bitwise XOR, so 2 ^ 3 equals 1. pow(2.0,3.0) computes the floating result 8.0. For small integer powers, checked multiplication may be the more appropriate representation.

questions.question: Why must getchar return int rather than char?
answer: It must distinguish every possible unsigned-char byte value from the separate EOF sentinel. A char may not preserve that distinction. Keep the result as int and check EOF before processing the byte.

questions.question: Why is isdigit(c) potentially invalid for a plain char?
answer: If char is signed, a non-ASCII byte may produce a negative value other than EOF. That is outside the ctype argument contract. Use isdigit((unsigned char)c) for stored bytes; preserve and separately handle EOF when reading through getchar.
